clue.text: In the beginning, outlaw was sturdy

indicators.note: the clue says one piece sits in the other, so the scrambled law goes inside the word for beginning

parts.note: a start is the beginning of something

indicators.note: the setter splits outlaw so that out, meaning disordered or wrong, works on the word law that follows it

explanation.surface: A tale of an outlaw who was a tough, sturdy figure from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outlaw' must be split as 'out' plus 'law': 'out' scrambles LAW into ALW, and 'In' puts ALW inside START. 'was' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalwart describes someone strong, robust and dependable, a synonym for sturdy.

clue.text: Say nothing: a fault at confession

parts.note: sh is the call for silence, an instruction to say nothing
a rift is a fault or split, as in rock

explanation.surface: A penitent says nothing about a failing at confession.
explanation.walkthrough: SHRIFT is an old word for confession to a priest, still heard in 'short shrift'. 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrift is an archaic term for confessing to a priest and receiving absolution.

clue.text: Collection not generally accepted in church? That's almost untrue

definitions.text: Collection not generally accepted in church

indicators.note: almost says the word for untrue is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: apocryphal means of doubtful truth, so a story called untrue can be described this way

explanation.surface: A doubtful story about a church collection is dismissed as nearly untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the final L of APOCRYPHAL. The books of the Old Testament that most Protestant churches leave out of the canon go by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocrypha are biblical writings excluded from the accepted canon by many churches.

clue.text: Suet cooked in salt develops a second skin

indicators.note: in says the reworked suet is placed inside the word for salt

parts.note: salt is wit, as in Attic salt, sharp humour

indicators.note: cooked means altered or falsified, so the letters of suet are reworked

explanation.surface: Suet prepared in salt grows a fresh layer of skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salt' here is the old sense of sharp humour, as in Attic salt, not the seasoning; 'develops' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A diver's rubber suit fits close to the body like an extra layer of skin.

clue.text: Latin beat Polish, master held in article

indicators.note: held in says the letter for master is held inside the word for polish

parts.note: to polish is to rub
M stands for master, as in the degree MA
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Advice to someone learning Latin to polish up, with the master keeping them in the classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latin' is the Latin American dance music, not the language; 'Polish' is the verb to rub, not the nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a Cuban dance with a distinctive rhythm, Latin American music.

clue.text: Second vehicle involved in collision

parts.note: a truck is a goods vehicle

explanation.surface: A second vehicle has been caught up in a crash.
explanation.definitionFit: Something struck has been hit, as anything in a crash is.

clue.text: Exchange rate in dollars initially volatile

indicators.note: volatile means unstable and changeable, so the letters are thrown into a new order
initially picks the first letter of dollars

explanation.surface: A currency exchange rate shown in dollars is unstable from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'volatile' rearranges RATE + IN + D, the D from 'dollars initially'.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade-in is an old item given in part payment for a new one, a swap.

clue.text: American line about uranium attracting unhealthy interest

indicators.note: about says American and line go around the symbol for uranium

parts.note: US stands for United States, so American
RY is short for railway, a line
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: An American railway line around a uranium mine draws unwelcome attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unhealthy interest' is excessive interest charged on a loan, not morbid curiosity. 'attracting' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Usury is lending money at exorbitant rates, charging more than is fair.

clue.text: Prevent increase in size for digest

explanation.surface: Advice to stop something growing so it can be digested.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is keeping food in the stomach without vomiting. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrain something stops it growing; to hold food in the stomach without being sick is to retain and process it.

clue.text: Obliged to look at a couple of points

parts.note: to behold is to look at
E and N are two compass points, east and north

explanation.surface: Someone required to look at a pair of items.
explanation.definitionFit: Being beholden is being indebted to someone, under a duty of gratitude.

clue.text: Make fast return with evidence of ill-health of about seventy

indicators.note: return asks for the word meaning make fast to be turned round and read the other way

parts.note: to moor a boat is to make it fast, tie it up
running a temperature is a sign of fever or illness

explanation.surface: An instruction to hurry back home with a doctor's note showing illness in a seventy-year-old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns MOOR into ROOM. 'about seventy' is degrees Fahrenheit, the comfortable warmth of an indoor space; 'of about seventy' looks like a patient's age.
explanation.definitionFit: Normal indoor warmth is roughly seventy degrees on the Fahrenheit scale.

clue.text: Conventional usage acceptable in fashion note

indicators.note: in says the letter for acceptable is placed inside the run made by fashion and note

parts.note: to fashion something is to form or shape it
la is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale
U means upper-class, hence socially acceptable, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: A remark that a particular fashion note is now acceptable usage.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class, socially acceptable, comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A formula is a set form of words used by convention, a stock phrase or rule of procedure.

clue.text: Petty as Polyphemus?

explanation.surface: A jibe that someone small-minded resembles the Cyclops of legend.
explanation.walkthrough: Polyphemus is the Cyclops of the Odyssey, who had a single eye in his forehead. The other sense is the informal one of a small, insignificant place.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the word means small-time and insignificant, as in a hick town; literally it describes the Cyclops with his single eye.

clue.text: By water pressure, clear mouth of channel

parts.note: to spit is to clear the mouth by expelling its contents
a head of water is the height that gives pressure in a system

explanation.surface: Instructions for flushing out the mouth of a channel by force of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' is a link putting the pieces side by side. SPITHEAD is the stretch of water in the Solent off Portsmouth, on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Spithead is a strait at the eastern end of the Solent, a sea passage between the mainland and the Isle of Wight.

clue.text: Power of the interpretive artist

explanation.surface: Praise for the power of a performer who interprets music.
explanation.walkthrough: In mathematics the power a number is raised to is written as a small raised figure. 'of the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In algebra the raised index showing repeated multiplication goes by this name; a performer who interprets a composer's work is also called one.

clue.text: Skill in speaking? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: in speaking says the word for skill is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: know-how is practical skill or expertise

explanation.surface: Someone claims to have a gift for speaking, and is flatly contradicted.
explanation.walkthrough: KNOW-HOW and NOHOW sound the same when the silent K and W go unheard. The question mark admits the clue word is spoken; 'Quite the opposite' is the dialect reply 'not at all'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nohow is an informal or dialect word meaning in no way, not at all, a flat contradiction.

clue.text: Gawky senhorita is the gardening lady

indicators.note: gawky means clumsy and awkward, so the letters of senhorita are rearranged

explanation.surface: An awkward young Portuguese woman turns out to be a keen gardener.
explanation.walkthrough: Hortensia is a woman's name from Latin hortus, garden, and is also another word for the hydrangea. 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The name comes from the Latin for garden, so a woman so named is a lady of the garden.

clue.text: Out of place, but I'm to stay here in the middle

parts.note: taken as written, dropping the apostrophe
a stay is a prop or support

indicators.note: in the middle picks the central letters of here

explanation.surface: Someone protests they are out of place, but must remain here in the centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stay' looks like a verb meaning remain; it is a noun, a supporting prop. 'but' and 'to' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something improper is unsuitable or inappropriate to the circumstances.

clue.text: Designs from agency

explanation.surface: A note that plans come from an agency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Designs' is a verb: whoever designs to do something intends it. 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To intend is to have in mind, as one who designs to act does; and the method or instrument by which something is achieved is its agency.

clue.text: Cut lady's slip

parts.note: a slit is a cut
her is the possessive for a lady

explanation.surface: A lady's petticoat has been cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slip' looks like the undergarment; it is the verb to slide.
explanation.definitionFit: To slither is to slide unsteadily, like a snake.

clue.text: Corcoran was in charge of this cover-up

definitions.text: Corcoran was in charge of this

explanation.surface: Someone called Corcoran oversaw an attempt to hush up a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Corcoran commands the ship HMS Pinafore in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera. The second sense is the sleeveless apron-dress worn over clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Corcoran captains the ship in the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta named after it, and a sleeveless overdress protecting clothes is a garment that covers up.

clue.text: Little bits one chucks around

indicators.note: around says the word for chucks goes round the letter for one

parts.note: to fling is to chuck or throw
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone tosses small scraps about.
explanation.definitionFit: Filings are tiny particles rubbed off metal by a file.

clue.text: A Zoroastrian Shakespeare?

annotationWithheld.why: A Zoroastrian Shakespeare? (6), complete as the scan prints it: 'A Zoroastrian' defines PARSEE, but no reading found ties 'Shakespeare?' to the answer, so the wordplay cannot be shown

clue.text: Again, dress rule broken by boy

indicators.note: broken by says the word for rule is split open and the boy's name set inside it

parts.note: to reign is to rule as a monarch
Al is a short boy's name

explanation.surface: A dress code is again being broken by a schoolboy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dress' is the military sense of lining troops up, so 'Again, dress' means put into line once more.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress ranks is to put soldiers in a straight line, so doing it a second time is to bring them back into alignment.

clue.text: Shaft for agricultural implement, it's commonly said

indicators.note: commonly said points to a working-class way of speaking that drops the opening H sound

parts.note: a harrow is a frame dragged over ploughed land to break up the soil

explanation.surface: A shaft for a farm tool, as people usually put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commonly' means in common speech, where the H is dropped; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrow is a slender shaft shot from a bow.

clue.text: A coloured resin lying about in volcanic crater

indicators.note: lying about says the run made by a, coloured and resin is turned round to read the other way

parts.note: red is a colour, so to be coloured can be to be red
lac is a resin secreted by an insect, used for shellac

explanation.surface: A tinted resin is found lying around inside the mouth of a volcano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying about' turns A + RED + LAC round as one run, giving CAL + DER + A.
explanation.definitionFit: A caldera is the large basin formed when a volcano's summit collapses into its emptied magma chamber.

clue.text: One from Cuba has somewhat tragic upbringing

indicators.note: in a down clue upbringing means bringing the letters up, read from bottom to top
somewhat says only part of the word tragic is used

explanation.surface: A Cuban has had a rather sad childhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat' takes RAGIC from 'tragic' and 'upbringing' turns it round. 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuba is famed for hand-rolled tobacco, so a Havana smoke comes from there.

clue.text: Single reproduction in book on unfinished temple

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the book follows the temple
unfinished says the name of the temple loses its final letter

parts.note: the Parthenon is the great temple of Athena on the Athens Acropolis
Genesis is the first book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A bit of reproduction appears in a book about an ancient temple that was never completed.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means after, so the book follows the temple; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Parthenogenesis is reproduction from an unfertilised egg, with no mate needed, hence by one parent alone.

clue.text: Deserts from military district

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a ward is an electoral district of a town

explanation.surface: Soldiers desert from a military district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deserts' looks like a verb about soldiers going absent, but it is the noun in 'just deserts', what one deserves.
explanation.definitionFit: One's deserts are what one has earned, good or bad, so a recompense fits.

clue.text: Time on deck for manoeuvres by the Horse Marines?

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the word for time follows the word for deck

parts.note: to deck is to adorn or dress up
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Time spent on a ship's deck for drill by a regiment of seagoing cavalry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deck' looks like part of a ship; it is the verb to adorn. The Horse Marines are a joke unit, here mounted cavalry.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is the training of a horse in precise, controlled movements, the sort of drill a mounted unit would perform.
